vignette:
He is 63, a married man from Oceania who has spent most of his adult life working as a financial analyst, someone who once took pride in order, prediction, and the quiet confidence that comes from making sense of numbers. Before the accident, he describes himself as steady and practical. His days are structured around market reports, spreadsheets, and routines he has refined over decades. He likes leaving for work early, stopping for coffee from the same place, and reviewing figures before the office fills with noise. His wife has always teased him that he trusts data more than instinct. He used to laugh and agree.

The change begins on an ordinary weekday morning about two years ago. He is driving to work before sunrise, thinking about a meeting later that day and mentally reorganizing a presentation. The road is wet from overnight rain. At an intersection not far from the city, a truck runs a red light. He remembers the flash of headlights first, then the violent sound of metal collapsing inward. He says time becomes strangely stretched and sharply detailed at once. He can still recall the pressure of the seat belt across his chest, the taste of blood in his mouth, and the smell of petrol. For a few seconds, trapped in the car and unable to move his leg, he is certain he is about to die. He thinks of his wife, not in a dramatic way, but with a plain, terrible clarity: she will get a phone call; she will have to identify him. That thought stays with him more than the impact itself.

He survives with multiple injuries and spends weeks recovering. During the first months, everyone around him focuses on the physical healing. Colleagues send messages, his wife manages appointments, and family members tell him how lucky he is. He repeats that word too-lucky-because it seems expected, and because he knows it is true. But at night he jerks awake drenched in sweat, hearing the crash again before he knows where he is. Sometimes he wakes with his fists clenched so tightly that his hands ache. His wife reaches for him and he startles hard enough to frighten both of them.

When he returns to work, he expects normality to pull him back into himself. Instead, the office feels different, almost hostile in its unpredictability. The sharp ring of a phone or the slam of a filing cabinet sends a shock through his body. If someone approaches his desk without warning, his heart races before he can tell himself he is safe. He finds it harder to concentrate on the kind of detailed financial modeling he once did effortlessly. He rereads the same line of a report several times and realizes he has absorbed none of it because, in the background of his mind, he is seeing headlights again. He begins staying later at the office, not because he is working efficiently, but because tasks that used to take an hour now take three.

Driving becomes its own ordeal. At first his wife drives him to and from work because his leg is still healing, and he tells himself he prefers being practical. But when he is medically cleared to drive, he delays. He invents reasons-the traffic is bad, parking is expensive, public transport is more sensible. Eventually he forces himself behind the wheel and grips it so tightly his shoulders cramp. At intersections he scans compulsively in every direction, even after the light changes. If a truck appears in his peripheral vision, his chest tightens and he feels heat rush through him. More than once he has pulled over because he is trembling too badly to continue.

At home, his world becomes narrower. He avoids the route where the accident happened and grows irritable when his wife suggests visiting friends across town because the drive will require passing near that intersection. News reports of road fatalities make him abruptly leave the room. He no longer watches the action films he used to enjoy because collisions, sirens, or shattered glass leave him cold and nauseated. His wife notices that he sits facing doors in restaurants and scans parking lots before they walk across them. He notices it too, and hates that he cannot stop.

He also carries a persistent sense of guilt and humiliation that he struggles to explain. Part of him knows he did nothing wrong, yet he cannot shake the belief that he should have anticipated the truck, should have seen something sooner, should have prevented what happened. He is embarrassed by how frightened he feels in situations other people consider routine. A man who spent his career trusting calm judgment now feels ambushed by his own body. He becomes quieter with colleagues, turns down invitations, and says he is tired. In truth, he is exhausted-by broken sleep, by vigilance, by the effort of appearing composed.

His wife says he is here and not here at the same time. He sits beside her in the evening with a laptop open to market summaries, but often he is somewhere else entirely, his jaw tense, listening for sounds outside. He still goes to work, still meets deadlines, still speaks the language of forecasts and risk. But the accident has altered his sense of the world. What once seemed manageable and patterned now feels capable of turning lethal without warning, and he moves through each day as if bracing for impact.
